title: Optimizing threat expectancy change during exposure therapy for anxiety disorders
summary: Anxiety disorders are very common and can seriously affect people and society. A standard and effective treatment is exposure-based cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT). In exposure, people face feared situations in a planned and safe way to test if their concerns about the situation are realistic. However, not everyone gets enough better. Research suggests how we might improve this therapy. It is not enough that the feared event does not happen during exposure. People also need to update what they expect in the future. In other words, “I thought something bad would happen. It didn’t. So it may be less likely than I believed.” The goal is threat expectancy change: a lasting drop in how much they think that their concern will happen. The size of this change after an exposure is like a learning rate. This learning rate differs a lot from person to person. Some things get in the way of this learning, such as safety behaviors and thoughts that downplay the new experience. Our study tests a brief conversation right after each exposure to strengthen this learning and reduce unhelpful thinking. Patients with anxiety disorders will be randomly assigned to one of two groups. Both groups receive the same manualized exposure-based CBT. In one group, each exposure is followed by a short, structured post-exposure discussion designed to boost threat expectancy change. The other group receives exposure as usual without this extra step. Before treatment, all patients will report factors that might hinder learning. In the experimental group, these factors will be reviewed and discussed repeatedly during the post-exposure discussions

interventions.name: Active Comparator: Manualized exposure-based cognitive behavioral therapy with 15 double-sessions (incl. psychoeducation, exposure, self-management, booster)

Experimental group: Manualized exposure-based cognitive behavioral therapy with 15 double-sessions (incl. psychoeducation, exposure, self-management, booster, same content as comparator) + Post-exposure processing to enhance exposure-related learning rate

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Primary diagnosis of panic disorder, agoraphobia, social anxiety disorder, or specific phobia according to DSM-5.
At least mild anxiety symptom severity (PROMIS-Anxiety ≥ 20).
Outpatient status (i.e., outpatient psychotherapy with weekly sessions for 12 weeks and booster sessions possible).
Sufficient German language skills.
Informed consent.
Exclusion criteria:
Acute suicidality.
Current or history of bipolar disorder, psychotic disorder, or borderline personality disorder.
Current alcohol, medication, or drug dependence (except nicotine and caffeine; abstinence should be > 6 months).
Severe medical conditions that prevent regular participation in therapy or bias research question (e.g., brain damage).
Any other general contraindications for exposure or psychotherapy (see Pittig & Pittig, 2024).
Any other reason endangering adherence to treatment protocol (e.g., planned inpatient treatment, planned absence or relocation, etc.). 
Concomitant psychotherapy (inpatient or outpatient). 
Concomitant psychopharmacological treatment is permitted, provided there has been no change in medication type or dosage during the 3 months prior to study entry.
